strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful failure of image generators: transparent objects must reproduce geometrically related scene content rather than merely look glass-like. This is a useful contribution to physically constrained image synthesis.

Snellcaster combines explicit refractive ray tracing with synchronized perspective–panorama generation in a coherent way. The auxiliary panorama provides a practical mechanism for completing surfaces visible only through refraction or reflection.

The reported improvements over Flux inpainting are substantial: average masked PSNR increases from 11.24 to 17.10 dB and LPIPS decreases from 0.51 to 0.28, while overall image-quality scores remain competitive. Figure 3 visually supports improved correspondence between the background and refracted content.

Supplementary examples extend beyond spheres to five additional geometries and demonstrate control through refractive-index changes. These examples support the method's usefulness beyond the main illustrative setting.

The manuscript explains the main pipeline clearly and provides prompts, sampling parameters, implementation details, and runtime. It also acknowledges important limitations of its Blender reference images.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the central contribution. Ablations remove detail-preserving averaging, Laplacian pyramid warping, and time travel—components adopted from prior work—but do not remove panorama synchronization or compare iterative synchronization against rendering/warping followed by the same harmonization step. Consequently, the evidence does not establish how much the proposed generative coupling adds beyond explicit optical rendering.

The physical-fidelity evaluation is conditional on the method's own estimated geometry: Blender uses the same lifted RGBD scene, and unobserved surfaces are masked out. This is useful for checking visible-region consistency, but it does not validate scene geometry, reflected appearance, or the unseen-region completion that motivates the panorama. Histogram matching further limits conclusions about photometric accuracy.

Quantitative evaluation covers only six indoor prompts with a sphere, without reported seed variability or uncertainty. Additional shapes are evaluated qualitatively. Moreover, standard Flux generation can change the background and object placement despite sharing a random seed, making comparison against a reference constructed from the object-free image less controlled than the inpainting comparison.

Claims of optical accuracy exceed the guarantees of the implementation. A single panorama centered at the object approximates viewpoints across its surface, secondary reflections are omitted, and synchronization blends generated predictions with physically warped content rather than enforcing exact equality. The subsequent unconstrained harmonization model can alter the result. These are reasonable approximations, but their effects on final physical consistency are not measured.

There are reporting and reproducibility issues. Table 1's per-scene values differ from supplementary Table 2, and its reported aggregate does not match its displayed scene values; for example, the six PSNR entries average approximately 17.45 dB rather than 17.10. Exact Flux checkpoints and the status of the described 'finetuned' relighting model are also insufficiently specified. These are correctable issues, distinct from the central experimental limitations.

Overall, the useful problem formulation, coherent method, and visible improvements place the paper near acceptance. However, missing tests of the central synchronization mechanism and the restricted physical-validation protocol leave the supported contribution at the borderline rather than establishing a clear acceptance case.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful failure of image generation: transparent objects must depict geometrically consistent transformations of the surrounding scene. Enforcing refractive correspondences is a useful contribution beyond improving generic perceptual scores.

The combination of explicit ray tracing, synchronization of clean-image estimates, and a jointly generated panorama is technically coherent. The panorama provides a practical mechanism for completing surfaces absent from the original view while supplying reflection content.

The reported improvements over Flux inpainting are substantial: average masked PSNR increases from 11.24 to 17.10 and LPIPS decreases from 0.51 to 0.28. Figure 3 visibly supports improved background inversion and correspondence. Supplementary Figures 9–11 extend the qualitative evidence to five additional shapes and different refractive indices.

The manuscript explains its main assumptions and provides equations, prompts, sampling settings, supplementary quantitative ablations, and an approximate runtime of 126 seconds per perspective–panorama pair. It also appropriately acknowledges limitations of the Blender reference and generic image-quality metrics.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the central contribution of synchronized generation. Comparisons are against Flux variants without equivalent geometric information; there is no geometry-matched rendering/compositing baseline followed by the same harmonization, no final-step-only warping comparison, and no panorama-synchronization ablation. Consequently, the results establish the value of explicit geometry more convincingly than the necessity or benefit of the proposed joint generation procedure. This is particularly consequential because averaging, pyramid warping, and time travel are adopted from prior synchronization work.

The physical-fidelity evaluation primarily measures agreement with the same estimated RGBD geometry used by the method. This is useful for checking correspondence enforcement, but does not independently validate scene-level optical accuracy. Masking unobserved surfaces excludes the regions that motivate panorama completion, and histogram-adjusted grayscale comparison cannot establish correct radiometry. Reflection consistency and unseen-region completion receive qualitative rather than controlled evaluation.

Claims of optically accurate or physically correct output exceed the demonstrated guarantees. The method uses estimated, fixed background geometry, an object-centered panorama approximation, and only the dominant first reflection. Its final generative harmonization can modify the constrained image without a subsequent physics check. These are reasonable engineering approximations, but the manuscript does not quantify their effects or establish that final outputs retain the enforced correspondences.

Quantitative coverage is limited to six indoor prompts with spheres, with no clearly stated seed count, variability, or failure rate. The additional shapes are valuable qualitative evidence, but do not establish robustness to geometry errors or object placement. Table 3 also gives mixed support for the auxiliary components: removing pyramid warping slightly improves PSNR and LPIPS, while removing time travel improves CLIP and ImageReward.

There are correctable reporting and reproducibility problems. Tables 1 and 2 give different per-scene values for the proposed method despite identical reported averages; for example, kitchen PSNR is 20.33 versus 18.78. The relighting model is described as a finetuned Flux Kontext model without a precise checkpoint or finetuning specification, leaving the scope of the training-free claim unclear.

Overall, the clear visual improvement and useful problem formulation place this near the acceptance boundary. However, the absence of controls testing the main synchronization contribution, together with incomplete validation of panorama completion and final optical fidelity, prevents a confident acceptance recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful weakness of generative image models: transparent objects must refract recognizable scene content consistently, rather than merely look glass-like. This is a useful contribution to physically informed image synthesis.

Snellcaster combines geometry-derived refraction correspondences with synchronized perspective and panoramic generation in a coherent way. Using the panorama to supply otherwise unobserved refracted and reflected content is a valuable extension of existing synchronized-generation methods, although several supporting techniques are inherited from LookingGlass.

The qualitative evidence is convincing for the principal claim of improved refraction consistency. Figure 3 shows recognizable background structures with appropriate inversion and distortion, while Figures 9–10 extend the demonstration beyond spheres to several complex shapes.

The reported improvements over Flux inpainting are substantial: masked PSNR increases from 11.24 to 17.10 and LPIPS decreases from 0.51 to 0.28. The supplementary per-scene results show improvements on both metrics across all six scenes. Together with the visual evidence, these gains support a useful contribution and favor weak acceptance despite the evaluation limitations.

The manuscript explains the main pipeline clearly and supplies equations, prompts, sampling settings, additional ablations, and a runtime estimate. It also explicitly acknowledges limitations of the Blender reference and the need for approximate lighting harmonization.
weaknesses: The evaluation establishes agreement with the estimated scene more strongly than independent physical correctness. Blender uses the same lifted RGBD scene underlying the method's warps, and the fidelity metrics exclude unobserved surfaces. Consequently, these scores do not validate the panorama's completion of unseen content or reflection consistency. Standard Flux also generates different scene layouts, making comparison against the original scene's reference less controlled than the inpainting comparison.

The ablations omit the central architectural choices: there is no comparison without synchronized panorama generation, against an independently generated panorama, or against rendering/warping followed by generative harmonization. The reported ablations instead examine inherited averaging, pyramid-warping, and time-travel components. This leaves the incremental benefit of the main synchronization design insufficiently isolated; Table 3 also shows mixed quantitative effects for the supporting components.

Claims of optical accuracy are stronger than the approximation supports. A single object-centered panorama approximates views from different surface positions, which can introduce parallax errors for nearby geometry. Reflection is restricted to the dominant first reflection, and Eq. 13 uses first-interface Fresnel coefficients without documenting accumulated transmission losses through subsequent interfaces. Generative relighting subsequently changes the image without enforcing the optical constraints. These are reasonable practical choices, but the demonstrated result is improved plausibility rather than complete physical correctness.

Quantitative evaluation is limited to six indoor prompts with a glass sphere, without reported variation across random seeds or uncertainty estimates. The additional shapes and refractive-index sweep provide useful qualitative breadth, but robustness to depth errors, placement, and difficult geometry remains unmeasured.

There are correctable reporting and reproducibility issues. Tables 1 and 2 give different per-scene values despite identical aggregate results; for example, the kitchen PSNR is 20.33 versus 18.78. The exact Flux checkpoints and the relighting model also need clearer identification: the text mentions a finetuned Kontext model without specifying its training or provenance. These ambiguities complicate reproducing the complete pipeline and interpreting its training-free description.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful weakness of image generators: transparent objects must reproduce geometrically consistent views of the surrounding scene. Combining explicit refractive ray tracing with synchronized perspective and panorama generation is a useful, coherent contribution to geometry-aware image synthesis.

The qualitative evidence supports improved refraction consistency. Figure 3 shows recognizable background structures refracted through the generated objects where FLUX inpainting omits or distorts them. Figures 9–10 extend the demonstration beyond spheres to more complex shapes, and Figure 5 provides two encouraging real-image examples.

The reported evaluation covers 300 scene–object combinations. Table 1 shows substantial improvements in masked refraction metrics: 16.51 dB PSNR versus 12.68 dB for the strongest baseline on that metric, and 0.24 LPIPS versus 0.47. The comparison with inpainting is particularly informative because it receives the same background image and object mask.

The method is reasonably well explained, with explicit warping, blending, Fresnel combination, and latent-update equations. The supplement supplies prompts, implementation settings, runtime, and additional ablations, and acknowledges limitations of the Blender pseudo-ground truth.
weaknesses: The reference-based comparison is not equally meaningful for all baselines. Blender renders the background and geometry derived from the method's initial image, while text-to-image baselines generate their own scenes. Sharing a random seed does not align scene content, object placement, or geometry across models; Figures 3 and 9 visibly show these differences. Their PSNR/LPIPS scores therefore conflate optical inconsistency with ordinary scene differences. The inpainting comparison supports the contribution more directly, but the headline comparison overstates what is established against unrestricted generators.

The experiments do not isolate the benefit of synchronized generation over a simpler geometry-based pipeline. There is no baseline using the same refractive warp and scene completion followed by one final harmonization step, or applying synchronization only at the end. Since explicit warping already supplies the visible-region correspondences measured by the principal metrics, the incremental value of enforcing them throughout denoising remains uncertain.

Evidence for panorama synchronization, a central contribution, is limited. The refraction metrics explicitly exclude rays hitting unobserved surfaces—the regions this component is intended to improve. Table 2 reports only a 0.23 dB PSNR and 0.01 LPIPS advantage over removing panorama synchronization on six sphere scenes, without variability estimates. Qualitative examples suggest a benefit, but do not establish reliable completion or reflection consistency across the evaluated shapes.

Claims of optical accuracy need qualification. The panorama approximates the surrounding scene from a single object-centered viewpoint; reflection uses only the dominant first bounce, and the Fresnel mixture in Equations 12–13 uses the entry-interface coefficients rather than accumulated interface contributions along the refractive path. Subsequent generative harmonization is unconstrained by these equations. These are reasonable approximations for plausible images, but the manuscript does not quantify their consequences, particularly for nearby geometry and complex objects.

The assertion that improvements come without sacrificing image aesthetics or text alignment is too strong. Table 1 gives ImageReward of -0.32, below every unrestricted text-to-image baseline, and CLIP of 32.85, below several baselines. These metrics do not assess refraction correctness, but they also do not support the claimed general quality improvement. Table 4 likewise shows mixed quantitative evidence for individual refinements: removing Laplacian pyramid warping slightly improves PSNR and LPIPS.

Reproducibility and computational cost remain incompletely specified. The relighting stage is described as using a fine-tuned FLUX Kontext model without sufficient checkpoint or fine-tuning details, and the supplement reveals selection among 20 relighting candidates. The reported 126-second runtime covers perspective–panorama generation rather than a clearly itemized full pipeline. The five prompt variations and object scale/camera-placement conventions are also not fully documented.

Overall, the visible-region refraction improvements and practical synthesis idea are substantial merits. However, unequal reference comparisons and insufficient isolation of the synchronization contribution leave the scientific evidence near the acceptance boundary. These concerns, rather than limited benchmark breadth alone, determine the borderline recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful failure of image generators: refracted content must agree with directly visible scene content. Combining explicit optical correspondences with generative completion is a useful contribution to physically informed image synthesis.

Snellcaster presents a coherent, training-free core pipeline combining Snell-law ray tracing, perspective–panorama synchronization, and Fresnel blending. The panorama provides a practical mechanism for completing content unavailable in the original perspective image.

The qualitative improvements are convincing for visible-background refraction, including the sphere inversions in Figure 3 and more complex geometries in Figure 9. Across the reported 300 scene–object combinations, masked PSNR improves from 12.66 to 16.51 dB and LPIPS from 0.47 to 0.24 relative to FLUX inpainting, which receives the same background and object mask.

The manuscript provides equations, sampling settings, prompts, component ablations, additional object shapes, and two real-image examples. It also explicitly acknowledges limitations of the Blender reference and the trade-off introduced by relighting.
weaknesses: The quantitative comparison conflates reference matching with optical correctness for the text-to-image baselines. The Blender reference uses the particular object-free image and geometry supplied to Snellcaster, whereas independently generated scenes can legitimately have different backgrounds, object placements, and shapes. Using the same random seed does not establish correspondence, especially across different models. The inpainting comparison is more informative, but the broader baseline rankings cannot cleanly establish refraction fidelity.

The evaluation provides limited direct evidence for the central unseen-region completion claim. PSNR and LPIPS explicitly mask out rays hitting unobserved surfaces, and the reference lacks correct illumination and reflected background content. Consequently, these metrics largely exclude the regions the panorama is designed to improve. Table 2 shows only modest changes without panorama synchronization (18.21 to 17.98 dB; LPIPS 0.24 to 0.25), without uncertainty estimates. Qualitative examples support plausibility but do not establish accurate scene completion or reflections.

The incremental benefit of synchronization over a simpler graphics-assisted pipeline is unresolved. There is no comparison against rendering or warping the same background with the same geometry, completing missing content once, and applying the same harmonization. Since value-weighted averaging, Laplacian pyramid warping, and time travel are inherited from LookingGlass, this comparison matters for identifying the added value of the proposed synchronized generation.

Claims of optical accuracy exceed what the implementation guarantees. Estimated depth, a single object-centered panorama, dominant first-reflection modeling, and blending with unconstrained generated pixels introduce approximations. Subsequent generative relighting can further alter refracted structure. These are reasonable engineering choices, but the manuscript does not quantify their consequences; Figure 5 supplies only two qualitative real-world comparisons.

Some conclusions overstate the reported evidence, and implementation details remain incomplete. Table 1 does not support improved text alignment or preserved aesthetics across all baselines: Snellcaster scores 32.85 CLIP and -0.32 ImageReward, versus 34.56 and 0.08 for SD3.5. The supplement describes selecting among 20 relighting candidates, but the exact finetuned harmonization checkpoint and full pipeline cost are insufficiently specified. Overall, the demonstrated refraction improvement is worthwhile, but uncertainty about comparative validity and the distinctive synchronization contribution leaves the paper near the acceptance boundary.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful failure of image generators: transparent objects must refract identifiable surrounding content consistently. Combining ray-traced correspondences with a jointly generated panorama is a useful approach to incorporating both visible and unseen scene content.

The qualitative comparisons in Figures 3, 9, and 10 show convincing improvements in refracted structure and object geometry over ordinary generation and masked inpainting, including nonspherical objects.

Table 1 reports substantial improvements across 300 scene–object combinations: 16.51 dB PSNR versus 12.15–12.68 for the baselines, and 0.24 LPIPS versus 0.47–0.53. The inpainting comparison is particularly informative because it shares the object-free background.

The manuscript explains the main synchronization procedure clearly, supplies prompts and important hyperparameters, and includes component ablations, refractive-index variations, and two illustrative comparisons with real photographs.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not adequately isolate the contribution of synchronized generation beyond explicit rendering. The method and Blender reference share the estimated RGBD scene and object geometry, whereas the text-to-image baselines can generate different backgrounds, shapes, and placements; identical random seeds do not establish correspondence. A geometry-matched rendering/compositing baseline with the same completion and harmonization resources is absent. This matters because several synchronization mechanisms are adopted from LookingGlass and SyncTweedies.

The central panorama contribution is only partially validated. The fidelity metrics exclude rays reaching unobserved surfaces, precisely where panorama completion is intended to help. Removing panorama synchronization changes PSNR from 18.21 to 17.98 and LPIPS from 0.24 to 0.25 on six sphere scenes, without uncertainty estimates. The qualitative evidence is useful, but does not establish reliable consistency of unseen content or reflections.

Claims of optical accuracy exceed the implemented guarantees. A single panorama approximates views from different surface positions, reflection modeling retains only the first reflection, and averaging with unconstrained generated estimates does not enforce exact ray consistency. Subsequent learned relighting can further alter the refracted region; Table 2 shows PSNR falling from 18.21 to 17.10 after this step. These are reasonable approximations, but support physical plausibility more strongly than physical accuracy.

Claims of improved text alignment and preserved aesthetics are not supported consistently by Table 1. The proposed method's CLIP score is below three baselines, and its ImageReward score of -0.32 is below all four text-to-image baselines. These metrics do not negate the refraction improvement, but the manuscript overstates what they demonstrate.

Reproduction of the complete pipeline remains uncertain. The relighting model is described as fine-tuned without sufficient checkpoint or training details, and the supplement uses 20 relighting candidates with PSNR-based selection. The reported 126-second perspective–panorama generation time does not establish total cost including this selection and preprocessing. Exact scene variations, seeds, and some geometry-placement details are also insufficiently specified.

Overall, the visible improvements and useful problem formulation place the paper near acceptance, but the missing geometry-matched baseline and limited direct validation of panorama synchronization leave the distinctive methodological contribution insufficiently separated from the benefits of rendering. These evidence and attribution concerns, rather than evaluation breadth alone, determine the borderline recommendation.
